blocks.text: It was now late in the afternoon, and sunset was not far off. We had to accept that we could do no more. With heavy hearts, we agreed when the Professor said:—

“Let us go back to Madam Mina—poor, poor dear Madam Mina. We have done everything we can do just now. At least we can protect her there. But we need not lose hope. There is only one more box of earth, and we must try to find it. Once we have done that, everything may still turn out well.” I could see that he spoke as bravely as he could to comfort Harker. The poor fellow had completely broken down. Every now and then he gave a low groan which he could not hold back. He was thinking of his wife.

We returned to my house with sad hearts. Mrs. Harker was waiting for us there. She seemed cheerful, which showed how brave she was and how she put others first. When she saw our faces, her own became as pale as death. For a second or two she closed her eyes, as if praying silently. Then she said cheerfully:—

“I can never thank you all enough. Oh, my poor darling!” As she spoke, she took her husband’s grey head in her hands and kissed it. “Lay your poor head here and rest it. Everything will still turn out well, dear! God will protect us if that is what He chooses in His goodness.” The poor fellow groaned. His suffering was so great that there was no place for words.

We ate supper together, though we gave the meal little attention. I think it cheered us all a little. Perhaps it was simply the warmth that food gives hungry bodies. None of us had eaten anything since breakfast. Or perhaps being together helped us. Whatever the reason, we all felt less miserable. The next day no longer seemed completely without hope. As we had promised, we told Mrs. Harker everything that had happened. At times she became as white as snow, when we described danger that had seemed to threaten her husband. At other times she turned red, when our story showed his deep love for her. But she listened bravely and calmly. When we described how Harker had rushed at the Count without thinking of the danger, she held tightly to her husband’s arm. It was as if holding him could protect him from any harm that might come. However, she said nothing until we had finished telling her everything, right up to the present moment. Then she stood up among us and spoke, still holding her husband’s hand. Oh, I wish I could give some idea of that scene! There stood that sweet, sweet, good, good woman. Her youth and lively spirit shone with beauty. There was a red scar on her forehead, and she knew it was there. We ground our teeth when we saw it, remembering where it came from and how she had received it. Her loving kindness stood against our fierce hatred. Her gentle faith stood against all our fears and doubts. And we knew what the signs meant: despite all her goodness, her purity, and her faith, they showed her as someone God had shut out.

“Jonathan,” she said. The word was so full of love and tenderness that it sounded like music on her lips. “Jonathan dear, and all you, my true, true friends, I want you to remember something throughout this dreadful time. I know that you must fight. You must destroy, just as you destroyed the false Lucy so that the true Lucy could live after death. But you must not do this work out of hate. That poor soul who has caused all this misery is the saddest case of all. Just think how joyful he will be when his worse part is destroyed too. Then his better part may live for ever as a spirit. You must feel pity for him too, though that pity must not stop you from destroying him.”

As she spoke, I could see her husband’s face grow dark and tight. It was as if the fierce feeling inside him was drying up his whole being, right to its centre. Without thinking, he held his wife’s hand more tightly, until his knuckles looked white. I knew she must be in pain, but she did not pull away or show it. Instead, she looked at him with eyes that begged him more strongly than ever. When she stopped speaking, he jumped to his feet. He almost tore his hand from hers as he said:—
